# EFS and FSx: say it

<!-- speak:start id=efs-fsx-s02 -->
### Prompt 1

**A customer asks.** We are moving our Windows file server, with all its share permissions, to AWS. Can we just use EFS like our Linux team does?

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**In 10 seconds.** No. EFS doesn't support Windows instances. FSx for Windows File Server gives you managed SMB shares that join your Active Directory.

**In 60 seconds.**

The short answer is no. EFS doesn't support Windows instances.

Use FSx for Windows File Server. It's a managed Windows file server with SMB shares.

It works like this. You join the file system to your Active Directory domain.

Your users sign in with their domain accounts, as they do today.

File and folder permissions are normal Windows permissions, so your current ones move with the data.

You copy the files with AWS DataSync, or with Robocopy.

A DNS alias lets people keep the old share name.

The thing to watch is the directory.

FSx joins AWS Managed Microsoft AD or your own Active Directory. AD Connector and Simple AD don't work.

In your case, the directory decides the plan.

Where does your Active Directory run today, on premises or in AWS?

**Skeleton.** EFS: no Windows / FSx for Windows: SMB shares / join your Active Directory / not AD Connector

**Must say.**

- Using Amazon EFS with Windows-based EC2 instances is not supported.
- FSx for Windows File Server provides fully managed Windows file servers and supports the SMB protocol.
- You join the file system to your Active Directory domain, which gives user authentication and file- and folder-level access control.
- The file system joins AWS Managed Microsoft AD or a self-managed Active Directory; Amazon FSx does not support AD Connector or Simple AD.
- FSx uses standard Windows ACLs, and an existing ACL configuration migrates without modifications; AWS recommends DataSync for the copy, with Robocopy as an alternative.

**Do not say.**

- "EFS works on Windows if you install an NFS client.". Say: Using Amazon EFS with Windows-based EC2 instances is not supported. Use FSx for Windows File Server.
- "You have to recreate all the share permissions.". Say: FSx for Windows File Server uses standard Windows ACLs, and you can migrate an existing ACL configuration without modifications.
- "AD Connector is enough for FSx.". Say: Amazon FSx does not support AD Connector or Simple AD. Join AWS Managed Microsoft AD or a self-managed Active Directory.

**Follow-up questions.**

- What happens if one Availability Zone fails? Choose a Multi-AZ file system. It fails over to a standby file server in a second zone, typically in less than 30 seconds. A Single-AZ file system usually has about 30 minutes of downtime during recovery.
- Is there a size limit for one file system? Yes. One file system holds up to 64 TiB. You can increase its storage capacity later, but you cannot decrease it.

</details>
<!-- speak:end -->

<!-- speak:start id=efs-fsx-s01 -->
### Prompt 2

**A customer asks.** A volume, a file system or a bucket for these files: how do I decide?

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**In 10 seconds.** It depends on who reads the files. One instance: a volume. Many Linux instances: a file system. Code that calls an API: a bucket.

**In 60 seconds.**

The short answer is: it depends on who reads the files, and how.

It works like this. A volume is block storage for a single instance.

A file system like Amazon EFS is shared. Many Linux instances mount it at the same time.

They can run in every Availability Zone of the Region. The code still reads and writes a normal directory.

A bucket in Amazon S3 stores objects. Your code reads and writes them through an API.

The thing to watch is the client. EFS is for Linux instances, not for Windows.

A bucket helps only if the code can use that API.

In your case, the report code writes to a directory, and it can't change this year.

So I'd mount one EFS file system on every instance.

Could the report code move to the S3 API next year?

**Skeleton.** who reads the files / volume: one instance / file system: many Linux instances / bucket: code calls an API

**Must say.**

- Amazon EBS is block storage for a single EC2 instance or container; Amazon EFS is file storage; Amazon S3 is object storage.
- File system storage fits applications that need shared read and write access across multiple EC2 instances or containers.
- EC2 instances in multiple Availability Zones of the same Region can access one EFS file system at the same time.
- Object storage gives access to data through an API, so code that writes to a directory has to change before it can use Amazon S3.
- Using Amazon EFS with Windows-based EC2 instances is not supported.

**Do not say.**

- "One EBS volume can be shared by all the web instances.". Say: Block storage is for a single EC2 instance or container. Many instances that share files need a file system such as Amazon EFS.
- "Amazon S3 works like a disk, with no code change.". Say: Amazon S3 is object storage that the code reaches through an API. Code that writes to a directory has to change to use it.
- "EFS works for Windows instances too.". Say: Using Amazon EFS with Windows-based EC2 instances is not supported. Windows file shares belong on FSx for Windows File Server.

**Follow-up questions.**

- Do we need a mount target in every Availability Zone? You can create one mount target in each Availability Zone, and all instances in that zone share it. Create one in each zone where your instances run.
- Does the file system fill up like a disk? No. You do not provision storage capacity for Amazon EFS. The file system grows and shrinks automatically as you add and remove files.

</details>
<!-- speak:end -->

<!-- speak:start id=efs-fsx-s03 -->
### Prompt 3

**A customer asks.** Our training data is 200 terabytes in S3, and our GPUs wait on data. Should we copy everything to EFS first?

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**In 10 seconds.** No copy needed. Link FSx for Lustre to the bucket. The file list comes first, and file data loads when a job first reads it.

**In 60 seconds.**

The short answer is no: link FSx for Lustre to the bucket instead.

Both are file systems that Linux instances mount. Lustre is built for speed, like machine learning.

It works like this. You link a Lustre file system to your S3 bucket.

The objects show up as files, so the training code reads a normal path.

A file's data loads from S3 the first time a job reads it.

Results can go back to S3.

The thing to watch is the deployment type.

A scratch file system doesn't replicate data. If a file server fails, that data is gone.

So the bucket stays your safe copy.

In your case, link the file system to the bucket you already have.

If a training run fails halfway, can your job read the data from S3 again?

**Skeleton.** both shared Linux file systems / Lustre built for speed / link to bucket, load on read / scratch: no replica

**Must say.**

- FSx for Lustre is for workloads where speed matters, such as machine learning and high performance computing (HPC).
- A Lustre file system linked to an S3 bucket presents the objects as files and can write file system data back to S3.
- An object's content is imported only when its file is first accessed, so the bucket is not copied before the job starts.
- On a scratch file system data is not replicated and does not persist if a file server fails; on a persistent one data is replicated and failed servers are replaced.

**Do not say.**

- "Lustre copies the whole bucket before the job starts.". Say: The content of an S3 object is imported only when its file is first accessed.
- "Scratch file systems are backed up for you.". Say: Backups are not supported on scratch file systems, because they are designed for temporary storage.
- "EFS is the fastest choice for GPU training.". Say: AWS names FSx for Lustre for workloads where speed matters, such as machine learning and HPC.

**Follow-up questions.**

- What if the data has to stay on the file system for months? Use a persistent file system. Persistent file systems are for longer-term storage and throughput-focused workloads. Their data is replicated, and failed file servers are replaced.
- Can our Windows laptops mount the Lustre file system? No. AWS lists Linux as the client for FSx for Lustre. Windows clients can use FSx for Windows File Server, FSx for NetApp ONTAP or FSx for OpenZFS.

</details>
<!-- speak:end -->

<!-- speak:start id=efs-fsx-s04 -->
### Prompt 4

**A customer asks.** Our EFS bill grows every month, and most of the files are old. What can we do without touching the application?

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**In 10 seconds.** Turn on a lifecycle policy. EFS then moves unread files to cheaper storage classes, with no code change.

**In 60 seconds.**

The short answer is: turn on a lifecycle policy on the file system.

It works like this. New files land in EFS Standard.

When a file goes unread for a set time, EFS moves it to Infrequent Access.

Infrequent Access costs much less to store.

Later it moves to Archive, for data read a few times a year.

It's a setting on the file system, not in your code. AWS gives you default times.

The thing to watch is reads. Reading a cold file adds a data access charge.

And by default, a cold file stays cold, even after someone reads it.

If old files get busy again, set the policy to move them back on first access.

In your case, I'd start with the defaults.

How often does anyone open a file that's older than a month?

**Skeleton.** lifecycle policy, no code change / Standard, then IA, then Archive / reads cost extra / move back on first access

**Must say.**

- EFS lifecycle management automatically transitions data between storage classes according to the lifecycle configuration of the file system.
- With a lifecycle policy at default settings, a file unread for 30 days moves to EFS IA, and one unread for 90 days to EFS Archive.
- EFS IA offers up to 95% lower cost than EFS Standard for infrequently accessed data.
- Reading files in IA or Archive adds data access charges, and by default files stay in IA or Archive after they are read.

**Do not say.**

- "The files move back to Standard by themselves when someone opens them.". Say: By default, files stay in IA or Archive when they are read. Set Transition into Standard to move them back on first access.
- "Cold storage is free to read.". Say: You are billed data access charges when files in IA or Archive are read.
- "You have to change the application to use Infrequent Access.". Say: Lifecycle management transitions data between storage classes according to the lifecycle configuration of the file system.

**Follow-up questions.**

- Which class fits files that people open a few times a year? EFS Archive. AWS designs EFS IA for data accessed a few times a quarter, and EFS Archive for data accessed a few times a year or less.
- Does Archive change anything about our throughput mode? Yes. EFS Archive is supported on file systems with Elastic throughput. While the file system has a lifecycle policy that moves data to Archive, you cannot change the throughput mode to Bursting or Provisioned.

</details>
<!-- speak:end -->
